newsitem.title: USA: Dow lower at midsession as rate woes intensify.
newsitem.headline: Dow lower at midsession as rate woes intensify.

text.p: Wall Street stocks were broadly lower Tuesday as rising interest rates weighed heavily on the market.
The Dow Jones industrial average was down 32.33 points at 6,534.85 at 1 p.m. EST. Declines led advances 13-10 on the New York Stock Exchange on volume of 295 million shares.
The Nasdaq Composite index, however, added 1.04 points to 1,317.44.
The benchmark 30-year U.S. Treasury bond lost 3/8 point, or $3.75 per $1,000 face value, boosting its yield to 6.80 percent, its highest in more than two months and up from 6.77 percent Monday.
"The fly in the ointment right now is interest rates," said Scott Bleier, chief investment strategist at Prime Charter Ltd. "A test of 7 percent may be in the cards."
Long term interest rates above 7 percent tend to draw money from the stock market.

Recent indicators have suggested economic growth is running at a stronger-than-expected pace. This initially had stocks and bonds responding in opposite fashion, with stocks benefiting from the prospect of stronger corporate earnings but bonds hurt by the fear of heightened inflation.
As bond values continued to erode, however, rates eventually pushed high enough to weigh on stocks.

"It seems like over the last few weeks, stocks had uncoupled from bonds," said Guy Truicko, portfolio manager at Unity Management. "But now it's looking like bonds want to head to 7 percent, and that's a crossroads for stocks."

The morning sell-off took the Dow index down more than 50 points, triggering trading curbs on the New York Stock Exchange. Shortly after midday, however, blue chip stocks halved their losses, leading the NYSE to lift the curbs shortly after noon.
Interest rate-sensitive sectors such as banking and financial service stocks were broadly weaker, with Citicorp off 1-3/4 to 102 and Chase Manhattan Corp. down 1-1/8 to 86-1/4.
Cyclical sectors like transportation, which benefit from a strong economy, shrugged off the effects of higher rates.
UAL Corp., which owns United Airlines, rose 1-1/8 to 60-7/8, and AMR Corp., parent of American Airlines, climbed 1-7/8 to 86-1/2.

Delta Air Lines inc. rose 1-1/8 to 71. The company said it would reorganize its European route structure, resulting in a one-time charge of up to $60 million. Delta expects the changes to boost its annual operating income by $62 million.

Santa Fe Pacific Gold Corp. rose 7/8 to 15-1/8 after receiving a sweetened takeover offer from Newmont Mining Corp. Newmont, which raised its offer to 0.4 of a share for each Santa Fe share, fell 1 to 40-1/4. Newmont had previously offered 0.33 of a share.
Homestake Mining Co., which has its own merger agreement with Santa Fe Pacific, rose 1/2 to 13-5/8.
